title: The False Witness and the Clay Dog (ES)
summary: A false witness testifies that he saw a theft committed in pitch-black darkness. Birbal uses a clay dog to shatter the perjurer's testimony. [ES]
full_text:
A greedy landlord named Seth Hiralal accused a poor tenant farmer of sneaking into his stables on a stormy, moonless night and stealing an ox.

To prove his case, Hiralal brought a hired witness—a shady gambler named Jaggu—who swore on the holy river: 'Your Majesty, I saw the theft with my own eyes! At two o'clock in the morning, during the pitch-black new moon, while torrential rain fell, I was standing fifty paces away and I clearly saw this tenant untie the ox and lead it into the woods!'

The poor tenant cried out his innocence, swearing he was asleep in his hut with his children.

Akbar was inclined to believe the eyewitness testimony. Birbal stepped in:

'Your Majesty, allow me to question this remarkable witness.'

Birbal asked Jaggu: 'You say you saw the theft at two in the morning, during a moonless, stormy night, from fifty paces away?'

'Yes, my lord! My vision is sharp as a hawk!'

Birbal pointed to a small wooden table in the corner of the council hall, thirty paces away, where a small clay statue rested.

Birbal asked: 'Jaggu, in this brightly lit hall, tell the court: what animal is depicted by that clay statue on the corner table?'

Jaggu squinted and replied: 'It is a clay dog, my lord!'

Birbal walked to the table, picked up the statue, and showed it to Emperor Akbar and the court:

It was an intricately carved clay lion, with a thick mane, fangs, and a curved tail!

Birbal smiled with razor-sharp irony:

'Behold, Your Majesty! In this brightly lit palace hall, in broad daylight, from only thirty paces away, this man cannot tell a lion from a dog!

'Yet he expects this court to believe that in the pitch-black darkness of a midnight storm, without a single lamp, from fifty paces away, he recognized the exact face of the tenant farmer in the rain!

'A hired liar always overreaches his script, forgetting that nature makes sight impossible in the dark!'

Jaggu broke down in terror, confessed that the landlord had paid him twenty silver coins to bear false witness, and begged for mercy.

Akbar ordered the landlord heavily fined, the false witness imprisoned, and the innocent farmer acquitted, praising Birbal's brilliant cross-examination.
